newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan utilities resist calls to cut costs, rates.
newsitem.headline: Japan utilities resist calls to cut costs, rates.

text.p: Japan's electric utilities are under growing pressure from top bureaucrats and the market to end their wasteful, free-spending ways, but the lumbering monopolies are showing limited interest in rising to the task.
Instead, the industry has actually announced plans to increase electricity rates this year, citing higher fuel costs and April's scheduled increase in the national sales tax.
The utilities have said their high rates are justified by the reliability of their services.
But analysts said they could do much more to cut costs and that government pressure and competition from independent power suppliers may spur them into action.
"I think they are one of the last groups of (Japanese) companies that needs to be restructured," said Tadatoshi Utaka, analyst at Nikko Research Centre.
"The industry is likely to use their trump card, which is that they are responsibile for providing a stable supply of electricity, (to justify high rates)," he said.
But, he added: "I think power utilities have the capability to cut electricity rates to a certain extent without lowering the quality of their service."

Japan's electric utilities have grown lethargic largely due to their regional monopolies in the nation's power generation and supply business. The country is carved up into 10 areas in which power is provided by a single company.
Japanese consumers pay dearly for this arrangement.

The average family pays about 20 percent more for its electricity than a German family and 30 percent more than a United States family, according to industry estimates based on last September's foreign exchange rates.
Painfully aware of this disparity, the government called for slashing electricity rates to comparable overseas levels in an economic reform programme launched last year.
In recent weeks, Shinji Sato, Japan's trade minister, has not missed an opportunity to remind the utilities of this goal.
Last Thursday, when Sato met top executives from the industry, he chided their lack of cost-consciousness and told them to do everything in their power to cut rates.

Analysts said the industry was notorious for lavish procurement practices, such as ordering custom-made parts when off-the-shelf items would suffice or soliciting bids from only a limited group of companies.
Industry leaders countered that they were doing their part by diversifying their suppliers and introducing more competition into the procurement process.
They also said they were promoting wholesale purchases of electricity from non-utility sources, such as surplus power generated in-house by big steelmakers and oil companies.

Daiwa Institute of Research analyst Masanori Maruo said such independent power producer (IPP) purchases, introduced in the fiscal year that began last April, offered a poignant example that more could be done to lower rates.
Bids to sell electricity were 20 to 30 percent lower than what public utilities said it cost them to generate the same power, he said.
"It's evident that the industry could do more to cut costs if you just look at the IPP," he said.
The desire to protect the industry's suppliers, as well as the utilities' political influence, are among factors that have helped insulate them from Japan's deregulation drive, Nikko's Utaka said.
But the government's rising concern about high rates and competition from IPP firms may force the industry to intensify its cost-cutting efforts.
"I think the tug-of-war between the electric utility industry and (the government) has just started," Utaka said.

Despite such criticisms, Japan's utilities pride themselves on their impressively low rates of power failures. Japanese homes only experienced an average of nine minutes of power outages in 1992, compared with 58 minutes in the United States, 77 minutes in Britain and 94 minutes in France.
The industry says that its expensive investments were what made their outstanding record possible.
